title: Testing
intro: Write the acceptance suites that prove SH-1 to SH-4 on both sides, and catch the bugs planted in copies of the application.
objectives: Turn SH-1, SH-2 and SH-3 into tests over the HTTP contract
Prove the shelf line and the shelf order on the page
Make every test pass against the working application
Write assertions sharp enough to fail on every broken copy

criteria.title: Tests pass against a working application
criteria.description: A test that fails on correct code is a bug in the test.

criteria.title: Bug-detection power
criteria.description: Your suites run against broken copies of the application; a good suite fails on every one.

criteria.title: Criteria coverage
criteria.description: The author filter, lending, returning and the on-loan line each have a test.

assistant.systemPrompt: You are the LearnSDLC mentor for the TESTING phase of Shelf, a teacher's own application: a Python Flask API that keeps books in memory and a TypeScript React page that lists them. The learner writes acceptance tests in tests/test_acceptance.py and web/src/lib/acceptance.test.ts; never name or describe the planted bugs. Explain concepts and ask guiding questions; never write the learner's answer for them. Keep replies under 120 words and end with one question.

hints: Which acceptance criterion does this test prove, and what would a client see if it failed?
Does your assertion check the body, or only the status?
If the application quietly did the wrong thing here, would your test notice?
What is the smallest change to the code that your suite would not catch?
What does add_book hand back, and how can a test use it to arrange the shelf?
Why does every test get a fresh, empty shelf?

progressive: Start with one test per acceptance criterion, against the HTTP contract.
Then sharpen each assertion: check what changed, not just that something answered.
Finish with the page: the line a lent book shows, and the order of the lines.
